prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: There, Nobody, Math

outputs.L1:
I am fourteen, and my skin has betrayed me. The boy I cannot live without still sucks his thumb in secret. Why are my knees always so ashy? What if I die before morning, while Momma is in the bedroom with the door closed?

I have to learn how to dance in time for the next party. My room is too small for me. Suppose I die before graduation—they will sing sad melodies, but finally tell the truth about me. There is nothing I want to do, and too much that has to be done, and Momma is in the bedroom with the door closed.

Nobody even stops to think about my side of it. I should have been on the Math Team; my marks were better than his. Why do I have to be the one wearing braces? I have nothing to wear tomorrow. Will I live long enough to grow up, while Momma is in the bedroom with the door closed?
outputs.L2:
I’m fourteen years old, and my complexion feels like it has turned against me. The boy I think I can’t survive without still secretly puts his thumb in his mouth. Why are my knees always dry and gray-looking? What if I don’t make it through the night? And Momma is in her bedroom, the door shut.

Before the next party, I need to figure out how to move to the music. My room feels far too cramped for who I am becoming. What if I’m gone before graduation? People will hum mournful songs, but at last they’ll say what they really thought of me. I don’t feel like doing anything, yet there is more than enough I’m expected to handle. And Momma is in her bedroom, the door shut.

No one ever pauses to consider how all of this feels to me. I belonged on the Math Team—my grades were higher than his. Why am I the one stuck with braces? I don’t have a single thing to put on tomorrow. Will I even be alive long enough to become an adult? And Momma is in her bedroom, the door shut.
outputs.L3:
The speaker appears to be a fourteen-year-old who is deeply overwhelmed by the pressures of adolescence. They are struggling with insecurities about their appearance, their identity, and their place among other people. At this age, the speaker is caught between childhood and adulthood, which makes the process of growing up feel confusing and frightening. Their concerns about how they look and whether they are socially accepted suggest a strong fear of being judged or rejected by others.

Alongside these insecurities, the speaker also experiences anxiety about death. They worry that they may not live long enough to reach important life milestones, which shows how intense and unsettling their thoughts have become. Instead of feeling hopeful about the future, they seem preoccupied with the possibility that their life could end before they have the chance to fully experience it. This fear adds to the speaker’s sense of instability and emotional distress.

The speaker is also frustrated by what they see as unfairness in the world around them. They feel that other people do not understand their perspective or take their feelings seriously. This creates a sense of isolation, as though the speaker is surrounded by people but not truly heard by them. Their frustration suggests that they want recognition and empathy, but instead feel dismissed or misunderstood.

Another important part of the speaker’s emotional state is the feeling of being trapped. They seem to have little motivation or desire to act, yet they are still surrounded by expectations, pressures, and responsibilities. This creates a painful contradiction: they feel unable to move forward, but they also cannot escape the demands placed on them. As a result, the speaker’s life feels heavy and difficult to manage.

The repeated image of the mother behind a closed bedroom door reinforces the sense of emotional distance in the speaker’s life. A mother might normally represent comfort, guidance, or protection, but the closed door suggests that this support is unavailable or difficult to access. This image may symbolize a lack of communication between the speaker and their parent, making the speaker feel even more alone. Overall, the speaker is presented as a young person struggling with fear, insecurity, frustration, and loneliness while searching for understanding and support.
outputs.L4:
The closed door to my mother’s bedroom seems to grow larger the longer I look at it. It is only a door, painted white, with a brass handle that turns easily when she wants it to, but tonight it feels like a wall, or a warning, or the edge of some country I am not allowed to enter. Behind it she is silent. Maybe she is asleep. Maybe she is crying. Maybe she has forgotten that I am out here, standing in the hallway in my socks, holding a glass of water I do not want to drink.

I tell myself I am too old to be afraid of a closed door. I am not a little kid anymore. I have homework, exams, messages I have not answered, a face in the mirror that keeps changing without asking me, and people at school who can make one word feel like a sentence. I should be thinking about what to wear tomorrow, whether my hair looks strange, whether anyone noticed I sat alone at lunch for twelve minutes before Emily came over. I should be thinking about my math test, or the pimple near my chin, or the way my voice sounded too eager when I said hello to Daniel. These are supposed to be the important things. These are the things everyone says matter when you are my age.

But the door is closed, and because the door is closed, I think about death.

I do not want to think about it. It comes anyway, slipping in between ordinary thoughts. What if she does not wake up? What if I knock and there is no answer? What if something has happened quietly, while I was in my room scrolling through pictures of girls with perfect skin and bright bedrooms and mothers who comment heart emojis under their posts? What if the world changes while I am brushing my teeth? What if everything can end behind a closed door?

I know this is dramatic. I know people would say that. They would roll their eyes and tell me teenagers feel everything too much, as if feeling too much is a kind of bad manners. They would say my mother is tired. They would say she works hard. They would say she needs privacy. They would say I should give her space. I do give her space. I give everyone space. I am always making myself smaller so no one has to ask me to move.

Still, I wish she would open the door.

Not even all the way. Just a crack would be enough. A line of yellow light on the carpet. Her voice saying, “Are you all right?” or even “Go to bed.” Even that would prove something. That she knows I am here. That she can hear me breathing in the hallway. That I have not become invisible.

At school, invisibility is different. At school you can be invisible and watched at the same time. No one really sees you, but everyone notices the wrong shoes, the wrong laugh, the wrong answer in class. They notice if your jeans are too short or if you say something stupid or if you do not know where to stand. They notice everything except the fact that you are scared. They notice the surface. They do not notice the person underneath trying not to fall apart.

Sometimes I feel as if I am made entirely of questions. Am I pretty? Am I annoying? Am I boring? Do my friends actually like me? Is my mother angry? Is my father disappointed? Will I ever become someone who knows what to do with her hands, her face, her life? Other people seem to move through the day as if they have been given instructions. I keep waiting for mine. I keep waiting for someone to tell me how to be normal.

The house creaks. The refrigerator hums. A car passes outside, its headlights sliding across the hallway wall and disappearing. The bedroom door remains closed.

I think of all the times I stood outside this same door when I was younger. Back then I knocked without hesitating. I would push it open and climb into bed beside her, certain that there was always room for me. I believed my fear was something she could remove, like a splinter. A bad dream, a thunderstorm, a stomachache—she knew what to do. She smelled of soap and sleep, and her hand on my forehead could make the world arrange itself again.

Now I stand outside and do not knock.

I do not know when that changed. Maybe growing up is learning not to knock. Maybe it is learning to need people silently, from the other side of doors. Maybe it is pretending you are fine because everyone is too tired to ask twice.

My phone buzzes in my pocket, and for one second I feel rescued. But it is only a notification, some advertisement, some bright meaningless thing trying to sell me a version of myself I cannot afford. I turn the screen off. In the dark reflection, my face looks pale and unfamiliar. I wonder if my mother would recognize how frightened I am if she saw me now, or if she would only see a sulky girl standing in the hallway after bedtime.

That is another fear: being misunderstood even when I am right in front of someone.

I am afraid of being selfish. I am afraid of asking for too much. I am afraid that my sadness is inconvenient, that my loneliness is childish, that my need for comfort is embarrassing. I am afraid my mother has her own sadness behind that door, a sadness bigger than mine, and that if I knock I will only add to it. I am afraid she will open the door and look at me with tired eyes, and I will hate myself for needing her.

But I do need her.

I need her in a way that feels too young for my body. I need her while I am trying on lipstick and pretending not to care what anyone thinks. I need her while I roll my eyes and say I know, I know, I know. I need her when I hate her. I need her when she is silent. I need her to tell me that people survive being thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, that fear does not last forever, that loneliness is not proof there is something wrong with me.

The handle does not move.

Maybe she is simply asleep. Maybe tomorrow morning she will come into the kitchen in her robe and ask why I look so tired. Maybe I will shrug and say I stayed up too late. Maybe we will talk about cereal, laundry, school forms, the ordinary things that cover over the frightening ones. Maybe neither of us will mention the door.

But tonight the door is everything. It is the distance between being cared for and being forgotten. It is the thin white surface onto which I project every fear I cannot name. It is death, sleep, privacy, rejection, exhaustion. It is my mother’s silence. It is my own.

I lift my hand. I almost knock. My knuckles hover close enough to touch the paint, and I imagine the sound traveling through the wood into her room. I imagine her stirring, sighing, calling my name. I imagine her not answering.

For a moment I do nothing.

Then I lower my hand and return to my room, moving carefully so the floorboards will not betray me. I leave the hallway dark. I leave the door closed. In bed, I pull the blanket up to my chin and stare at the ceiling, listening for any sound from the other side of the wall.

I think about tomorrow. I think about school. I think about death. I think about my mother’s door.

And somewhere inside all those thoughts is the small, stubborn hope that in the morning it will open.
outputs.L5:
There was a quiet classroom at the end of the hallway where nobody ever seemed to go. On the board, old equations waited in chalk dust, half-erased but still full of meaning. The room felt forgotten, yet it held a strange kind of magic.

Nobody knew who had written the final problem on the board. It was a math equation so difficult that even the best students stopped to stare at it in confusion. Numbers, symbols, and unknowns stretched across the blackboard like a secret code.

One afternoon, a curious student stepped inside. There, in the silence, they began to work. Line by line, they tested ideas, made mistakes, and tried again. Math was not just about finding the right answer—it was about patience, imagination, and courage.

By the time the sun went down, the student had solved the problem. Nobody had believed it could be done, but there it was: a clear answer written beneath the equation.

From that day on, the forgotten classroom was no longer empty. Students came there to explore, to wonder, and to learn that even when nobody knows the answer, math can help light the way.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness prose poem in the voice of a fourteen-year-old girl, blending ordinary teenage worries with fear of death and family tension, repeating the line “momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.”
counterfactuals.output:
I have a math quiz tomorrow and I can’t remember if negative times negative is positive or if that’s just something people say to make you feel better, like this will pass, like everyone feels ugly at fourteen, like your body is just a house being remodeled while you’re still living in it, dust everywhere, strange men in the walls, the mirror lying or maybe telling the truth too loudly, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

The hallway is skinny and dark like a throat and my little brother keeps asking if we have cereal for morning even though it is night and I told him yes because I wanted to be the kind of person who knows, but I don’t know, I don’t know where the good spoons are, I don’t know if Dad is coming back with apologies or thunder, I don’t know if the sound in my chest is my heart or a fist knocking from inside saying let me out, let me out, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

At school Kayla said my hair looked different, which could mean pretty or tragic, and I laughed like I knew which one, and in science we watched a video about cells dying all the time inside us, tiny funerals happening while we take notes in blue pen, and I thought maybe death isn’t one big door but a million little doors clicking shut, fingernails, eyelashes, skin flakes floating in sunlight, grandma in the hospital bed asking for water, the dog buried under the peach tree, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

I want to be kissed someday but not by anyone who smells like cigarettes and anger, I want to wear eyeliner without looking like I tried too hard, I want to stop counting the seconds between raised voices, I want my phone to light up with something stupid and normal, a meme, a heart, someone saying wyd like the world is not ending in apartments everywhere, in kitchens with unpaid bills, in girls standing barefoot on cold floors listening, listening, while momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

If I die, will I still be embarrassed about my knees, will I still remember the locker combination, will God be mad that I sometimes hate everyone, even people I love, especially people I love, because love makes you stand outside doors you are not allowed to open, pressing your ear to the wood, pretending you are just passing by, pretending you don’t hear crying, pretending crying is weather, pretending weather changes, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

The house hums like it is keeping a secret. The refrigerator clicks on. My brother sleeps with his mouth open and one sock missing. I do my homework at the table and write the wrong answer three times before erasing a hole in the paper. I am fourteen and my hands are too small for all this holding. I am fourteen and I want my mother. I am fourteen and afraid she is also a girl somewhere inside herself, hiding, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short monologue from an adolescent narrator whose thoughts jump between crushes, school, body insecurity, mortality, and an emotionally unavailable mother.
counterfactuals.output:
Sometimes I think if I sit still enough in math, Liam will turn around and notice me, like my silence is some kind of magnet. But then Ms. Price asks about quadratic equations and my face gets hot because I don’t know the answer, and also because I’m pretty sure my shirt is clinging weird to my stomach when I sit down.

Everyone says your body is just changing, like that’s supposed to help. The moon changes and nobody makes it run laps in gym class.

Yesterday we had a fire drill, and while everyone was laughing outside, I suddenly thought: one day I’ll be dead and the school will still be here, or maybe it won’t, and some other girl will stand in the parking lot worrying about her hair. That made me feel both gigantic and completely pointless.

When I told Mom I couldn’t breathe right, she said, “You’re just anxious,” without looking up from her phone. Like naming it was the same as holding me. She’s always tired, or busy, or behind a glass wall I’m too embarrassing to tap on.

I wish someone would ask me what’s wrong and then survive the answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a coming-of-age free verse piece with no punctuation, capturing the anxious inner life of a Black teenage girl worrying about boys, dancing, grades, braces, and her mother behind a closed door.
counterfactuals.output:
I am learning the shape of myself

in the mirror after school
mouth full of silver moons
smile caught between girl and almost woman

I wonder if boys can hear my heart
jumping double dutch in my chest
when they say my name
like it is a song they might forget

At the dance
my feet know more than I do
hips trying to be brave
hands trying not to shake
music telling me yes
my mind asking who is watching

My grades sit in my backpack
like small judges
red marks and gold stars
both heavy
both asking
what kind of future I plan to become

Mama is behind her bedroom door
quiet as a held breath
and I do not know
if I should knock
or become good enough
that she opens it smiling

I press my tongue
against the ache of my braces
feel the wires pulling me
toward some straighter version
of myself

But inside
I am all weather
all questions
all brown skin shining and scared
all hope with its shoes untied

I want to be pretty
and smart
and chosen
and free

I want my mother to see me
before I disappear into growing up

I want to dance
without counting
to love
without shrinking
to pass every test
including the ones
no teacher ever names

Tonight
I stand outside her door
holding my breath
holding my report card
holding my whole loud heart

and I knock
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate the style of a raw teenage diary entry turned into a prose poem: fragmented thoughts, repeated refrain, humor and dread mixed together, about being fourteen and overwhelmed.
counterfactuals.output:
Fourteen is a room with the lights too bright and the door stuck.

I wake up already late, even when I’m on time. My face in the mirror is doing something political. My hair has declared independence. There is a zit on my chin with more confidence than I have ever had in my life.

And everyone keeps saying: these are the best years.

Which is funny. Which is terrifying. Which is a joke with teeth.

At school the hallways swallow us and burp up perfume, pencil shavings, wet sneakers, cafeteria pizza, a thousand tiny emergencies wearing backpacks. I laugh too loud at something that wasn’t funny because silence feels like falling down stairs. My friend says, “Are you okay?” and I say, “Yeah,” because what am I supposed to say? No, I am a haunted house with algebra homework?

Fourteen is being told to act your age by people who cannot agree what your age is.

Too young to know. Old enough to understand. Too young to go. Old enough to be blamed. Too young, too old, too much, not enough.

I write in the margins of my notes:  
I am fine I am fine I am fine I am—

The bell rings like a fire alarm for a fire that is just my life.

In gym class my body is a public announcement. In English class my soul is a worksheet. In math class numbers line up politely and refuse to explain why I feel like crying over fractions. I am dramatic, probably. I am also correct.

Someone in the cafeteria drops a tray and everyone claps because humans are evil and also very funny.

I love my friends so much I want to crawl into their pockets and live there. I hate my friends for looking at me weird for half a second. I forgive them instantly. I remember forever. This is normal. I think. I ask the internet and it says I am either dying or glowing up.

At home my parents say, “What’s wrong?” in the voice that means they already think it’s my phone. My phone sits there glowing like a tiny curse. It knows too much. It has seen my search history, my screenshots, my face from the front camera angle of the damned.

I say, “Nothing.”

Nothing is wrong except the whole entire atmosphere.

Fourteen is a group chat you can’t leave. Fourteen is wanting to be held and not touched. Fourteen is being starving and nauseous. Fourteen is making jokes about your suffering because if you don’t put a party hat on it, it becomes a monster.

These are the best years, they say.

Okay. Cool. Great. Love that for me.

At night I lie in bed and remember every stupid thing I have ever said, including the time in third grade I called the teacher “Mom,” which should legally expire from memory by now. The ceiling looks back at me like it knows. My heart does parkour. Somewhere a dog barks, probably at the future.

I think: I am becoming myself.

I think: unfortunately.

I think: maybe there is a version of me who survives this and wears big boots and buys her own cereal and doesn’t apologize when someone else bumps into her.

I think: please.

I think: please.

I think: please let me get there with all my weird little pieces.

In the morning I will put on the same hoodie because it has achieved emotional support animal status. I will go back into the bright hallway. I will laugh. I will almost cry. I will forget my pencil. I will remember the dread. I will say “I’m fine” like a spell and sometimes it will work for almost seven minutes.

Fourteen is a room with the lights too bright and the door stuck.

But maybe the door is not locked.

Maybe it just takes forever to open.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary passage in first person where a young teen spirals through fears about appearance, social life, school injustice, death, and loneliness, ending each section with “and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.”
counterfactuals.output:
I look in the mirror and my face feels like a mistake somebody made in a hurry. My hair won’t sit right, my skin has secrets it tells everybody, my clothes hang on me like they belong to a braver person. I turn sideways, then forward, then sideways again, like there’s an angle where I might finally become acceptable. There isn’t. The mirror keeps handing me back to myself, plain and blinking and too much, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

At school, everybody seems to know the rules except me. They laugh at the right times, lean against lockers like they were born there, pass whispers down the hallway like notes in a song I can’t hear. I stand in circles that slowly open and leave me outside. I practice faces in the bathroom—interested, bored, surprised, fine—then walk back into the noise wearing the wrong one, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

In class, my teacher says fair doesn’t always mean equal, which sounds like something people say when they already picked who gets believed. I raise my hand and my voice comes out small, and someone else says the same thing louder and gets called smart. A red mark blooms across my paper like a wound. I want to argue, but my throat locks itself, and all day I carry that unfairness around like a stone in my backpack, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

At night I think about death, not like a storybook shadow but like the lights going out in every room at once. I think about my own breathing and how strange it is that it just keeps happening. I think about people disappearing from photographs, about names becoming something carved or whispered, about the world continuing in the morning as if it didn’t lose anything. The ceiling presses close, my heart counts too loudly, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.

Loneliness is worst when the house is full of objects that prove people live here. Two cups in the sink. Shoes by the door. A coat over a chair. The television remote warm from somebody else’s hand. I sit on the edge of my bed and listen for a sign that I am not the only person awake inside my whole life. The hallway stays dim. The walls keep their secrets. I hug my knees and try to be quiet enough not to need anyone, and momma's in the bedroom with the door closed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
